newsitem.title: MEXICO: At least 14 injured in Mexico City fuel blast.
newsitem.headline: At least 14 injured in Mexico City fuel blast.

text.p: More than 3,000 people were evacuated from their homes on Tuesday as firefighters battled an inferno raging in three huge fuel storage tanks that exploded just outside Mexico City.

At least 14 people were injured in Monday afternoon's disaster, four of them critically. Towering columns of flame lit the Mexico City's night sky as clouds of thick black smoke billowed up three miles (five km) into the sky.

The fire began as workers from state oil monopoly Pemex repaired a valve in a tank containing 80,000 barrels of fuel at a storage facility but the exact cause was not known, Pemex chairman Adrian Lajous said early on Tuesday.
"We heard a loud noise, we didn't know what it was. Then we saw the fire," said a shaken Lourdes Rivas Mendoza, a 30-year-old housewife who lives near the site of the blast.
Firefighters trained hoses on skyscraper-high flames and other nearby tanks, hoping to stop the blaze from spreading. But the size of the inferno dwarfed their efforts.
Lajous said he expected the blaze to be extinguished sometime on Tuesday as 100,000 barrels of fuel in the tanks burned off. No property outside the Pemex storage area had been damaged, he said.
"We hope to put it out in the next few hours," he told private radio station Radio Red. "It depends on how fast we burn off all the fuel."

Company officials admitted that residents of the heavily populated area of San Juan Ixhuatepec, about 11 miles (17 km) north of central Mexico City, were still at risk from more tanks exploding until the flames were extinguished.
The thousands evacuated spent the night in temporary shelters or with relatives but some were already returning on Tuesday despite the danger, fearing their empty homes would be robbed.

Dozens of dazed firefighters, some struggling to stay on their feet, were treated for smoke inhalation by Red Cross workers. Some complained they lacked proper equipment to fight the massive blaze and had not even been fed properly during their round-the-clock shifts.

Doctors in area hospitals said most of the victims suffered second- and third-degree burns. Bloodied firemen were seen being taken on stretchers to hospitals, their faces raw with burns and swathed in bandages.

Mexican media were quick to point out that Monday's blast occurred at the same Pemex installation where a disastrous natural gas explosion 12 years ago burned at least 511 people to death and engulfed homes in a huge tongue of flame.
"Pemex again," headlined the Guadalajara daily Siglo 21 on its front page, over a picture of a thick column of smoke.

The accident was the third major disaster to hit Pemex in less than two years and Lajous said he would set up a special committee to study safety issues urgently because "Mexicans deserve a full explanation."

As millions watched the dramatic images of the blaze on special live television broadcasts, concern mounted that the thick smoke would worsen already serious winter pollution in one of the world's filthiest cities.

Environmental officials ordered schools to suspend all outdoor activities and recommended that pregnant women, babies and the elderly remain indoors to escape the toxic cocktail of fumes spreading over this city of 18 million.
Other tanks in the facility contained as much as 1.25 million gallons (4.7 million liters) of fuel each but were being slowly drained to prevent new explosions, officials at the oil giant said.
An unknown number of residents were treated for smoke inhalation and many complained of a burning sensation in their eyes, witnesses said.

Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, on a visit to South America when the tanks exploded, ordered federal emergency aid to the area. Chief spokesman Carlos Almada said Zedillo was being briefed constantly on the disaster and issuing instructions as he travelled.

The explosion was the second in four months at a Pemex installation. On July 26 a blast caused by human error at the firm's Cactus gas processing centre in the southern state of Chiapas killed six workers and caused a massive blaze, which could be seen for miles around.
